coverageMethod: A modern area's catalog representative point is tested against a hand-generalized historical reference envelope. Color means approximate geographic correspondence with the dated source map, not proof that the whole modern district or tehsil was governed uniformly.
note: Historical territories were not modern administrative units. These schematic envelopes are for comparison and omit small enclaves, frontier changes and local autonomy. Border areas can be misclassified. Sources describe nominal extent or a conventional historical reconstruction; the app does not turn these into surveyed historical borders.

empires.name: Mauryan Empire
empires.sourceTitle: India in 250 B.C., Charles Joppen's A Historical Atlas of India (1907), cartography by Justus Perthes
empires.author: Charles Joppen / Justus Perthes (historical reference map); OpenCarto (generalized coordinate envelope)
empires.license: Reference map: public domain (1907). Generalized coordinate envelope: CC0-1.0.
empires.method: Hand-generalized WGS84 longitude/latitude envelope from the grey Empire of Asoka region in the public-domain 1907 map, using its graticule and named cities as visual landmarks. Not a georectified trace. Yellow Kashmir and southern kingdoms in that particular map are excluded. The coastal details and internal autonomous areas are not resolved.
empires.note: This is the conventional territorial envelope in Joppen's 1907 reconstruction, not a claim of continuous direct administration. Monica L. Smith's 2005 archaeological study explains why network-based interpretations and Ashokan inscription distributions do not establish uniform territorial control. The Deccan and northwestern frontier are particularly uncertain; several later reconstructions differ from this map.

outside.name: Srinagar (excluded in this source's grey envelope)

empires.name: Mughal Empire
empires.sourceTitle: Mughal Empire, Late Seventeenth Century, Figure 3 in India: A Country Study, Library of Congress Federal Research Division (1995)
empires.author: Library of Congress Federal Research Division (reference map, based on Joseph E. Schwartzberg's atlas); OpenCarto (generalized coordinate envelope)
empires.license: Reference map: public domain U.S. federal government work. Generalized coordinate envelope: CC0-1.0.
empires.method: Hand-generalized WGS84 longitude/latitude envelope using the government map's approximate empire limit and named places, with large frontier bends retained. This reference is dated late seventeenth century rather than an exact 1707 snapshot. Not a georectified trace; colonial ports and small enclaves cannot be distinguished at this scale.
empires.note: The source explicitly calls the limit approximate and marks independent Pathan tribes and peoples in revolt. The colored modern units therefore represent nominal geographic extent, with uneven authority and contested Deccan control. European settlements such as Goa and Madras are not separately cut out of modern districts. This is not a claim that every place inside was under direct Mughal administration in one particular year.

empires.name: Sikh Empire
empires.sourceTitle: Map showing the extent of Sikh territory at the death of Maharajah Runjeet Sing, John Walker (c. 1846), read alongside the Wallace Collection's Ranjit Singh exhibition research
empires.author: John Walker (historical reference map); Davinder Toor / Wallace Collection (curatorial context); OpenCarto (generalized coordinate envelope)
empires.license: Historical reference map: public domain (c. 1846). Generalized coordinate envelope: CC0-1.0. Wallace Collection text is cited for context, not reproduced.
empires.method: Hand-generalized WGS84 longitude/latitude envelope from the map's pre-partition Sikh extent, using its graticule, Sutlej, Indus and named towns as landmarks. The 1846 post-war partitions are not treated as the 1839 border. Broad Punjab, Peshawar, Kashmir and Ladakh reach is checked against the Wallace Collection's curatorial description. Not a georectified trace.
empires.note: The historic map also shows intricate cis-Sutlej possessions and frontier relationships that cannot be faithfully assigned to entire present-day districts. This coarse envelope retains the main connected territory; small detached possessions and tributary arrangements are omitted. Patiala and the other protected cis-Sutlej states are not colored wholesale. Himalayan and tribal frontiers remain uncertain, and modern disputed boundaries are not adjudicated by this overlay.
